/cards/0/segments/0/text: [[NPC1]]'s father made his fortune in cloth, and earned his neighbours' dislike along with it. Their house stood near the great square, but that did not make it easier for his daughter to enter the life of the city. She stammered and was not considered pretty. Her mother was determined to make her sociable; the less progress she saw, the sharper her ridicule became.
/cards/0/segments/1/text: Before they went out, her mother hung {{e_jewels|Jewels}} upon her, one piece after another. Gold and silver could not speak for her. They served instead as a conspicuous harness, exposing every shrinking movement to the room. She lived alone with her thoughts. Suitors began to call; what they saw in her fortune was easier to explain than what they saw in her.
/cards/0/segments/2/text: She insisted that she would never marry. Mother and daughter quarrelled, accused each other, slammed doors. She believed that if she held her ground on this one matter, some part of her life might remain her own. Her resistance lasted until she was twenty-six. It ended in marriage to an impoverished, haughty nobleman.
/cards/0/segments/3/text: At the wedding the church was full of the guests' whispered mockery. The cloth merchant's money had purchased a title, but the title could not shield her from their looks. In time she had a great house and servants, and people were obliged to address her formally as the Marquesa. Only the habit of sitting alone, waiting for someone to want her company, survived the change in rank.
/cards/0/segments/4/text: Years later she placed all her hopes upon another little girl. The child's name was {{e_clara|Clara}}, and her beauty seemed almost unbelievable. At last there was someone she could love without reserve. She had not yet learned how to let that person grow freely.
/cards/1/segments/0/text: I can hear them. The church in {{e_lima|Lima}} is so large, and so many people are speaking softly. Every word seems far away and right against my ear. If I do not look up, I need not discover whose face is laughing. I have put on the clothes they wanted me to wear and married the man they were willing to accept. Why have I still not done it right?
/cards/1/segments/1/text: Mother dislikes the way I speak. When I am nervous, a word has to strike against my mouth several times before it comes out. People have already begun to feel impatient, or embarrassed for me. Yet alone I have so much to say. Without interruptions I can think a thing through, even invent a remark that might make someone laugh. When I sit before them, the remark is gone.
/cards/1/segments/2/text: Once I thought I would never marry. With the door shut, it still seemed possible. When the door opened again, the accounts, the relations and the suitors were all waiting outside. I did not know quite whom they were waiting for.
/cards/1/segments/3/text: These {{e_jewels|Jewels}} are still here. They attract attention more easily than my words. How I wish that one day someone would come to my side simply because they wanted to sit with me for a while. I would never let that person feel lonely again. They call me señora. I still do not know how to lift my head.
/cards/2/segments/0/text: By the time [[NPC2]] was eight, she could calmly correct her mother's choice of words. She resembled her father: clever, composed, able to watch another person's agitation without sharing it. [[NPC1]], meanwhile, grew increasingly afraid of her daughter's startled looks. She tried to be gentle, tried to please, watched for every need—and invariably offered the thing before the child had wanted it.
/cards/2/segments/1/text: Such attentions were difficult to refuse. Reject one small favour and it seemed that you had rejected all the love behind it; accept reluctantly, and the next enquiry followed. The daughter grew weary, the mother alarmed. After an argument two doors closed, and the same house suddenly became enormous. Sitting alone, the mother rehearsed their conversation over and over, searching each time for a sentence that might bring her daughter back.
/cards/2/segments/2/text: People would later call this daughter heartless. Yet as an adult she generously helped friends, servants and gifted strangers, tending to them as if they were her children. Her coldness was not bestowed equally upon everyone. Before the one person who most longed for her tenderness, she felt she must first defend a little distance.
/cards/2/segments/3/text: More proposals arrived. The mother imagined someone joining their life; the daughter considered how to leave it. The marriage she finally chose required her to settle in {{e_spain|Spain}}. It was not the next street. A letter sent there might wait half a year for an answer.
/cards/2/segments/4/text: Little by little the luggage was packed. The doors that had once closed after quarrels would stand open after the daughter left. Her mother could add another possession to a trunk, ask whether something might be needed on the journey. None of these small errands could abolish the sea already lying between them.
/cards/3/segments/0/text: {{e_clara|Clara}} has shut the door again. I know I should not go to it at once. Asking through the wood whether she is angry will only make her angrier. But if I never ask, how will she know I am waiting?
/cards/3/segments/1/text: I am not angry when she corrects me. She is so clever; I ought to be pleased. I am only a little afraid. Once I have said something wrong, whatever follows seems to require her permission. So I talk still more, explaining a small matter at great length, until the weariness I most dread appears on her face.
/cards/3/segments/2/text: As a child I feared a door suddenly opening too: Mother coming in to ask why I was standing like that again, why I could not be like other girls. How have I made my own child want to escape her room? Surely what I give her ought to be different from what I received.
/cards/3/segments/3/text: If she would come out and say she did not blame me, I could be quiet. She need not even say it. She could sit beside me. {{e_loneliness|Loneliness}} was mine alone, yet I keep requiring an answer from her before I can believe that today may pass. I listen to the sounds behind her door. Even I can see that this waiting must distress her. When the room grows quiet, I am more frightened still.
/cards/4/segments/0/text: Before the ship sailed, a blessing was given. For so distant a journey, embraces and waving could not be enough: people aboard and people ashore knelt together and sang a hymn. The wide sea received their voices without making them stronger. The singing sounded thin, hesitant. Already the water between the hull and the shore was widening.
/cards/4/segments/1/text: [[NPC1]] was perfectly composed. She had chosen a marriage that would take her to {{e_spain|Spain}}, and was moving towards the life she had chosen. Behind her, her mother stood on the shore, pressing a hand now to her heart, now to her mouth, as though the farewell might retain its dignity if only she could keep something from bursting out of her chest.
/cards/4/segments/2/text: The sailing ship grew brighter before [[NPC2]]'s eyes, while its outline grew less distinct. Tears streaked the tranquil Pacific. The huge pearl-coloured clouds seemed as if they would remain there forever. People could sail away beneath them, however, to a place where one could not knock on a door at any moment or hear an immediate reply.
/cards/4/segments/3/text: The daughter aboard showed none of the distress her mother hoped to see. Composure might mean courage before a voyage, or relief at having at last obtained distance. From the shore, one could not judge by so remote a figure. The mother watched until the ship no longer allowed her to distinguish anyone on its deck.
/cards/4/segments/4/text: In time, {{e_letters|Letters}} would travel between the two continents. Sailing dates would become the measure of her life, and the few sentences her daughter chose to write would be unfolded again and again. No amount of rereading would shorten this water. The ship too had received its blessing. No one had explained to the mother on the shore how to bring this farewell to an end.
/cards/5/segments/0/text: Four years have passed since we last parted. On the voyage here I told myself: do not rush towards her, do not weep, do not lay all those years of words upon {{e_clara|Clara}} at once. To live in the same house as her is already enough.
/cards/5/segments/1/text: She tried too. We both knew that some things should never have been said. This time, if I asked a little less and she was a little more patient, perhaps we could sit down to a peaceful meal. Before it was over I heard my voice change. She put down what she was holding. We had returned to the moment we knew best.
/cards/5/segments/2/text: Dawn has not yet come in {{e_spain|Spain}}. She sleeps behind the door; I stand outside it. If I wake her, there will be another farewell, more explanations, more tears over words I had meant to say lightly. Let her sleep. I press my lips to the door, just once. It does not open. This time I do not knock.
/cards/5/segments/3/text: When I am home again, paper will be quieter than I am. A mistaken sentence can be crossed out; an urgent one rewritten. She need not watch me struggle to speak, and I need not see at once where she has grown tired of reading. Tomorrow must still be lived. The ship will not wait until I have finally learned to say goodbye.
/cards/6/segments/0/text: As the mailing day approached, [[NPC1]] ventured out again. She endured dinners and looks in the street, listened to strange events at the {{e_court|Viceregal Court}}, read {{e_scripts|Spanish Plays}}, and sought a story or two for her {{e_letters|Letters}}. She did not lack money or expect these compositions to win her fame. She wanted her daughter to smile suddenly as she read. She followed celebrated people such as {{e_camila|Camila}}, remembering the actress's reputation at the {{e_theatre|Theatre}}.
/cards/6/segments/1/text: {{e_clara|Clara}} had written that the king admired her {{e_goldchain|Gold Chain}} and asked her mother to send a similar one as soon as possible. Her mother turned the purchase into an adventure: at midnight she climbed into a painting, the painter reached through the colours to help her, and she explained to its inhabitants that the loveliest girl in the world wished to present a gift to the most courteous king. It was a joke in a letter. The only surface she could truly cross remained a sheet of paper.
/cards/6/segments/2/text: She wrote of her daughter's cold, of the gum sold by the nuns. After solemn advice she could not resist adding a sharp observation. Anxiety and wit sat side by side, like the two things she wanted to say: take good care of yourself; and spare another glance for your mother. As the night deepened she rearranged her sentences until the heavy wish appeared light.
/cards/6/segments/3/text: Before dawn, the envelope and presents were wrapped together to await the shipping agent. Once the letter left her hands, she often retreated into drink and sleep until the next mailing day drew near. The letters were chiefly preserved by her son-in-law, who admired their style. Her daughter generally glanced through them.
/cards/6/segments/4/text: Many years later, students would study these sentences and scholars would debate the making of her style. The woman at the desk was not looking so far ahead. She merely folded the paper, hoping that this time there might be some echo from across the sea.
/cards/7/segments/0/text: I wonder whether something here in my chest has truly gone wrong. If a physician opened it, could he see the traces of these years? I wrote the thought to {{e_clara|Clara}}. She reproached me for studying only myself and making a god of sorrow.
/cards/7/segments/1/text: From the balcony of the {{e_palace|Marquesa's House}}, it is easy to watch people kissing and greeting one another and suspect that they perform it for an audience. I know the thought is cruel. Still I ask myself: if they have not suffered as I have, what makes their love real?
/cards/7/segments/2/text: Then I am afraid to raise my eyes. I want her to love me, and to admit that I am better than other mothers. I wait for her to ask my forgiveness, as though every fault lay on her side. Even the reconciliation I imagine must end with her yielding.
/cards/7/segments/3/text: She has placed thousands of miles between us. I have no opportunity left to rule her, yet I am still wrestling with the desire. A page of tenderness does not mean that I can let go. But what else do I know how to do, except write another page?
/cards/8/segments/0/text: [[NPC1]] feared less for her own death than for the sickbeds, orphans and homeless women who would remain after it. Finishing her accounts at night, she often imagined a day when women might organise to protect women travelling alone, women in service, women in mines and workshops. In the morning she still had to go begging for this month's expenses.
/cards/8/segments/1/text: She began to look for a successor. Through wards, courtyards and corridors she hurried, inspecting face after face, disappointed by her own haste. At last she stopped beside the washing trough. A twelve-year-old girl was directing the others at their work while telling the miracles of Saint Rose of Lima with tremendous dramatic enthusiasm. That girl was [[NPC2]].
/cards/8/segments/2/text: From then on the least popular duties often fell to the girl. On journeys she carried eggs and vegetables; at home she learned how each part of the institution worked. Sometimes, in the middle of a task, the older woman in black would call her aside and discuss the arrangement of contagious wards, the management of people, or how to ask the wealthy for money. These were not merely orders. It was almost as if a colleague were being briefed.
/cards/8/segments/3/text: When {{e_maria|María}} came to borrow an orphan as a companion, the abbess saw an opportunity. The girl would encounter the world outside; perhaps the rich old woman could be turned towards useful work. She weighed the strain the arrangement would impose upon the girl and believed she knew when to draw back.
/cards/8/segments/4/text: At first the girl visited for occasional afternoons. Eventually she went to live there. Two years of training had taught her many responsibilities. No one had taught her with equal care how to admit that a burden was too much.
/cards/9/segments/0/text: Sometimes {{e_abbess|Mother Pilar}} comes to find me without warning. I am still holding the eggs when she begins to talk about the wards, about which two people will quarrel if put together, or whom we should ask for help so the journey will not be wasted. I thought such things ought to be said to other grown-ups. But she keeps looking at me, as if I can understand them too.
/cards/9/segments/1/text: I want to remember. Someone is waiting for everything she asks. The sick cannot miss a meal because I am afraid; the roof cannot keep leaking because money is hard to borrow. When I listen to her, those things feel close. Perhaps if I try a little harder, I can become the person she needs.
/cards/9/segments/2/text: Back in bed, though, I feel small again. When she asks whether I can manage, of course I say yes. If she knew I sometimes cried in secret, would she think she had mistaken me? At {{e_convent|Saint Rose's Convent}}, when I do not understand, I can wait for her to come near. How long will I have to wait in that lady's house?
/cards/9/segments/3/text: Everyone says I should be glad: it is a sign of trust. I am glad. I simply did not know that trust could weigh so much, or that, unlike a basket, it could not be set on the ground when my arms grew tired. What she wants me to remember goes far beyond today's errands.
